57.title: Hillel on one foot
57.hook: asked to teach the whole Torah on one foot, Hillel says: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor, the rest is commentary, go and learn (Talmud, Shabbat 31a)
57.howItsDone: Jews study Hillel's answer in the Talmud, Shabbat 31a, and it is often taught to children as a first summary of Jewish ethics, always together with its last words: go and learn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the swimmer went down with the swirl and came up singing: wu wei. Your line was go with the water. Where did you stop forcing? Day fifty-seven, and a new week: Jewish wisdom tales.

Somebody asks you to explain your whole job, your whole faith, your whole life's philosophy, in one sentence. Go. Right now. Elevator pitch. It's a slightly rude question, and a slightly brilliant one. Two thousand years ago, in Jerusalem, a man walked up to two of the greatest rabbis of his day with a version of it. The Talmud tells the story. He said: teach me the entire Torah, all of it, while I stand on one foot. The first rabbi, Shammai, chased him away. The second was Hillel. Today's story is Hillel on one foot.
screen: `EXPLAIN IT IN ONE SENTENCE.` → `TEACH ME ON ONE FOOT.` → `SHAMMAI, THEN HILLEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the scene, from the Babylonian Talmud, tractate Shabbat, page thirty-one. A man who isn't Jewish comes to Shammai and asks to be taught the whole Torah on one foot. Shammai, who is famously strict, pushes him away with the builder's measuring stick he's holding. So the man goes to Hillel, and asks the same thing. And Hillel doesn't send him away. He gives him an answer, in Aramaic, and it's short enough to say standing on one foot. What is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah. The rest is commentary. Now go and learn. Three things happen in that answer. First, the center. The Talmud doesn't name a verse here, but many readers hear behind it the commandment in Leviticus, in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society wording, "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself," put in its most practical form: don't do to others what you hate. You met a version of this on day fifteen of this path, the golden rule, and it lives in many traditions. Second, the rest is commentary. Not unimportant, but built around that center. And third, the part people forget, the last words: now go and learn. Hillel doesn't say the one line is enough. He gives the summary, and then sends the man to study. The whole teaching fits on one foot. Living it takes two feet and the rest of your life. Hillel and Shammai, the Talmud says, often disagreed, and their schools argued for generations. Jewish tradition kept both sides of their arguments, and remembers Hillel especially for his patience.
screen: `SHAMMAI PUSHES HIM AWAY.` · `WHAT IS HATEFUL TO YOU, DON'T DO.` · `THE REST IS COMMENTARY.` · `THE ONE LINE ISN'T THE END.` · then, large: `NOW GO AND LEARN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand on one foot and say it. If you can, stand up now. If standing isn't right for you, sit tall and lift one hand instead. Find your balance. Say it quietly: what is hateful to me, I won't do to my neighbor. Wobble if you wobble. Then put your foot down, and breathe. Think of one person you'll see today, and one thing you'd hate someone to do to you, that you might be tempted to do to them. The bell holds the time.
Zil g'mor, Aramaic for go, learn. Hillel's last words to the man standing on one foot, after summing up the whole Torah in a single line.
Your line: now go and learn. Today, live the one line once, on purpose. Then learn one new thing about something you thought you already understood. Day fifty-seven.

58.title: Honi and the carob tree
58.hook: an old man plants a tree that won't fruit for seventy years, for his grandchildren (Talmud, Taanit 23a)
58.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Honi in the Talmud, Taanit 23a, and it is a familiar retelling around Tu BiShvat, the new year of the trees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hillel taught the whole Torah on one foot, zil g'mor, and ended: now go and learn. What did you learn? Day fifty-eight.

Somebody planted the tree whose shade you last sat in. Somebody laid out the park, stocked the library, worked out the recipe a family still makes. They did it knowing they would never meet the people who'd use it. The Talmud has a story about this, and about a man named Honi. Tradition remembers him as a holy man in the land of Israel, known as Honi the Circle-Drawer, because once, in a drought, he drew a circle on the ground and would not step out of it until it rained. One day Honi is walking along a road, and he sees an old man planting a tree. Today's story is Honi and the carob tree.
screen: `SOMEONE STARTED IT FOR YOU.` → `HONI THE CIRCLE-DRAWER.` → `AN OLD MAN PLANTING A TREE.`

segments.voice: The story begins with a verse that bothered Honi. A psalm about the return from exile, which in the King James words reads: "When the LORD turned again the captivity of Zion, we were like them that dream." Seventy years in exile, like a dream. Can a person really sleep seventy years? So Honi is on the road, turning that over, and he sees the old man planting a carob tree. Honi asks: how long until this tree gives fruit? Seventy years, says the man. And Honi asks: are you so sure you'll live another seventy years? And the old man says, more or less: I found carob trees in the world when I came into it. My ancestors planted them for me. So I'm planting these for my children. Then Honi sits down to eat, and falls asleep. Rocks grow up around him, hiding him, and he sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that same tree. Are you the one who planted it? Honi asks. No, says the man. I'm his grandson. The Talmud's story goes on, and it ends sadly: back home, nobody believes he's Honi, and he feels so alone that he no longer wants to live. The rabbis draw from it a saying, companionship or death. But the heart of the first part is the old man, planting. He does the work, and the fruit belongs to someone he'll never meet. He got here under trees he didn't plant, and he knows it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plant or start something for someone later. For now, settle, and breathe, and look around. Find one thing near you that someone made or planted before you: a tree outside, a building, a word you use. Thank them silently, whoever they were. Then think of one small thing you could start today for someone after you. A seed in a pot. A note for your kids. Money set aside. A skill you teach. Pick one. The bell holds the time.

Your line: for the ones after. Today, do one small thing whose fruit you may never see. Plant it anyway. Day fifty-eight.

59.title: Why weren't you Zusya?
59.hook: Rabbi Zusya fears heaven won't ask why he wasn't Moses, but why he wasn't Zusya (Hasidic tale)
59.howItsDone: Zusya's question is retold in Jewish teaching and sermons, and Hasidic tales like it are still passed on aloud in Hasidic communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, an old man planted a carob tree, haruv, for grandchildren he'd never meet. Your line was for the ones after. What did you start for someone later? Day fifty-nine.

Scroll for thirty seconds and you'll find someone doing your life better than you. A better cook. A better parent. Someone your age who's already written the book, run the marathon, started the company. It's easy to feel like you're failing at being them. The Hasidic tales of Eastern Europe tell of a rabbi named Zusya. He was known for being poor, humble and full of joy. Near the end of his life, his students find him weeping, afraid. They're amazed. What could a man like Zusya possibly fear? Today's story is why weren't you Zusya?
screen: `SOMEONE DOING YOUR LIFE BETTER.` → `RABBI ZUSYA, WEEPING.` → `WHAT COULD HE FEAR?`

segments.voice: Rabbi, the students say, why are you afraid? You've been as faithful as Moses. As kind as Abraham. And Zusya answers: when I come before the heavenly court, they won't ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Moses? I'd have an answer for that: I wasn't given what Moses was given. They won't ask, why weren't you Abraham? I wasn't Abraham. They'll ask me: Zusya, why weren't you Zusya? And what will I say then? That's the whole story. It comes from the Hasidim, a movement of joyful, mystical renewal among the Jews of Eastern Europe. Their stories were told aloud before anyone wrote them down, and later collectors, Martin Buber among them, carried this one into print. Now notice what Zusya refuses to do. It's easy to measure yourself against the greatest person you can imagine, and against that measure, anyone comes up short. Zusya says that isn't the test. Nobody will ask you to be Moses. The question is harder and kinder at the same time: did you become the person only you could be? Did you use what you were actually given? Your hands, your voice, your odd mix of gifts and wounds? It's harder, because you can't hide behind I'm not Moses. It's kinder, because nobody is asking you to be anyone else. Zusya couldn't answer for Moses. He could only answer for Zusya.
screen: `WHY WEREN'T YOU MOSES?` · `A TALE FROM THE HASIDIM.` · `WE MEASURE AGAINST SOMEONE ELSE.` · `HARDER, AND KINDER.` · then, large: `WHY WEREN'T YOU ZUSYA?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing only you would do. For now, settle, and breathe. Let go of the person you've been comparing yourself to. Let them walk off. Then ask quietly: what do I have that's mine? A way of making people laugh. A particular kindness. Something you notice that others don't. Pick one, and think of one small way to use it today, the way only you would. The bell holds the time.
Zusya. A Hasidic rabbi who feared one question: not why weren't you someone greater, but why weren't you yourself.
Your line: be zusya. Today, when you catch yourself wishing you were someone else, stop, and do one thing the way only you would do it. Day fifty-nine.

60.title: Two pockets
60.hook: Rabbi Simcha Bunim keeps two notes: "for my sake the world was created" and "I am dust and ashes" (Hasidic tale, drawing on Sanhedrin 37a and Genesis 18:27)
60.howItsDone: Simcha Bunim's two pockets are taught in Jewish schools and sermons, and some people do carry the two notes; the lines come from Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 and Genesis 18:27.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Zusya feared one question: why weren't you Zusya? Your line was be zusya. What did you do that only you would do? Day sixty.

Two slips of paper. That's all today needs. On a bad day a person can feel like nothing: small, useless, invisible. On another day, the same person can feel like the center of the universe, the smartest one in the room, owed something by everyone. It's possible to swing between the two in a single afternoon, and to reach for the wrong feeling at the wrong moment. There's a Hasidic teaching for exactly this. It's told of Rabbi Simcha Bunim, a Hasidic master in Poland. He said every person should carry two pockets, each with a slip of paper inside. Today's story is two pockets.
screen: `SOME DAYS, NOTHING.` → `SOME DAYS, THE CENTER.` → `CARRY TWO POCKETS.`

segments.voice: In one pocket, a note that says: for my sake the world was created. In the other: I am dust and ashes. And the teaching is simply this: know which one to reach for. Both lines come from much older sources. The first is from the Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin. It asks why the Bible tells of one single human being created at the beginning, and answers, in part: to teach that a single life counts as a whole world. And so, it says, each person should say: for my sake the world was created. The second line is from Genesis. Abraham is standing before God, bargaining for the city of Sodom, pleading for any good people who might live there. And in the King James words he says he has dared to speak to the Lord, "which am but dust and ashes." Notice: Abraham says it while he is boldly arguing with God. Humility and courage in the same breath. So when do you reach for which? When you feel worthless, when you're crushed, when you think your life doesn't matter: reach for the first pocket. The world was made for you, too. Your life counts as a whole world. And when you feel proud, when you're sure you're above someone, when you're about to be cruel because you can: reach for the second. Dust and ashes. The trick isn't choosing one note forever. It's carrying both, and knowing which the moment needs. Neither is the whole truth alone. Together, they're a person.
screen: `FOR MY SAKE THE WORLD WAS CREATED.` · `I AM DUST AND ASHES.` · `ABRAHAM SAYS IT WHILE ARGUING.` · `CRUSHED? PROUD? CHOOSE THE NOTE.` · then, large: `REACH FOR THE RIGHT POCKET.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write both notes, one per pocket. If you have paper, tear two small slips. On one, write: for my sake the world was created. On the other: I am dust and ashes. Put one in your left pocket and one in your right. If you don't have paper, hold one hand, then the other. Settle, and breathe. Ask: which pocket does today need? Feel for it. The bell holds the time.
Two pockets. One note says the world was made for you; the other says you are dust and ashes. Reach for the one the moment needs. Today's word.
Your line: reach for the right pocket. Today, when you feel small, reach for the world made for you. When you feel too big, reach for the dust. Day sixty.

61.title: The boy with the whistle
61.hook: an unlettered boy whistles in the synagogue on Yom Kippur, and the Baal Shem Tov says his whistle opened the gates (Hasidic tale)
61.howItsDone: Jews observe Yom Kippur with a full day of fasting and prayer that ends with Neilah, the closing service, and the shofar's blast; the tale of the whistling boy is told in Hasidic communities and sermons around the holy day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two pockets: the world was made for you, and you are dust and ashes. Your line was reach for the right pocket. Which one did today need? Day sixty-one.

Have you ever been somewhere sacred, a wedding, a funeral, a service, and felt like you didn't know the words? Everyone else is singing along, standing and sitting at the right times, and you're mouthing something, hoping nobody notices. Today's story is for anyone who's felt that. It's a Hasidic tale, from Eastern Europe, told about the Baal Shem Tov, whom Hasidic tradition remembers as its founder. It's Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. The synagogue is packed. People have fasted and prayed since the night before. And at the back stands a village boy who can't read a word of the prayer book. Today's story is the boy with the whistle.
screen: `NOT KNOWING THE WORDS.` → `YOM KIPPUR, THE DAY OF ATONEMENT.` → `A BOY WHO CAN'T READ.`

segments.voice: The boy's father has brought him, worried. The boy is simple, the story says, a shepherd boy, and he has a little whistle he plays for the sheep. The father made him promise to keep it in his pocket. All day the boy stands there, watching everyone pray words he can't follow. He wants to join in. He has nothing to join with. It's growing late. The final prayer of the day has begun, the one the tradition calls Neilah, the closing, when the gates of heaven are pictured swinging shut. And the boy can't hold it in anymore. He pulls out his whistle and blows it, one loud, shrill note, right in the middle of the closing prayer. The whole room turns. People are furious. His father is mortified. And the Baal Shem Tov stops, and then he finishes the prayer, and afterward, the story says, he tells them: the gates were closed. All our prayers, all our learned words, were stuck. And that boy's whistle, from a whole heart, broke through, and carried our prayers up with it. That's the story, and it's been told in many versions. Hasidic tales like this one honor simple, heartfelt devotion alongside learning. Jewish tradition treasures study deeply; this tale doesn't reject it. It says the heart can get through too, even when the words won't come. The whistle got through because it was all the boy had, and he gave all of it.
screen: `A SHEPHERD BOY WITH A WHISTLE.` · `NEILAH: THE GATES CLOSING.` · `ONE SHRILL NOTE.` · `A WHOLE HEART BROKE THROUGH.` · then, large: `THE WHISTLE GOT THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks in your own clumsy way. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing you're grateful for today. Now, instead of finding perfect words, give thanks however it comes out. Hum a note. Tap your hand on your knee. Say thanks out loud, badly. If you pray, you can say it in your own words, however rough. It doesn't need to be beautiful. It needs to be yours, and whole. The bell holds the time.
Neilah, the closing prayer of Yom Kippur. A boy who couldn't read blew his whistle during it, and the Baal Shem Tov said it opened the gates.
Your line: the whistle got through. Today, when you don't have the right words, for a friend, for thanks, for sorry, offer what you have. Day sixty-one.

62.title: The treasure under the bridge
62.hook: Isaac of Kraków travels to Prague for a dreamed treasure and learns it's under his own stove (Hasidic tale)
62.howItsDone: The tale of Isaac of Kraków is told in Hasidic teaching about finding what's sacred close to home, and the old synagogue in Kraków's Kazimierz district that bears the name of Isaac son of Jacob is often linked to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, during Neilah, a boy's whistle broke through on Yom Kippur. Your line was the whistle got through. How did you give thanks, clumsily? Day sixty-two.

Somewhere out there is the thing that will fix everything. The better city. The better job. The retreat in the mountains. The person who finally gets you. We spend a lot of life planning the trip to go and get it. There's a Hasidic tale about a man who actually made that trip. His name was Isaac, the son of Yekel, a poor, devout man in Kraków, in Poland. Night after night, he dreams the same dream: go to Prague, and under the bridge that leads to the king's castle, you'll find a treasure. The third time he has the dream, he packs a bag. Today's story is the treasure under the bridge.
screen: `THE THING THAT WILL FIX EVERYTHING.` → `ISAAC OF KRAKÓW.` → `GO TO PRAGUE.`

segments.voice: It's a long walk from Kraków to Prague. When Isaac finally gets there, he finds the bridge. But it's guarded by soldiers day and night, and he doesn't dare dig. So he hangs around. Every day he comes back and circles the bridge, until the captain of the guard notices and asks, kindly enough, what he's looking for. Isaac, having nothing to lose, tells him about the dream. And the captain laughs. You walked all this way because of a dream? If I believed in dreams, I'd have gone to Kraków long ago! I keep dreaming there's a treasure under the stove of some Jew called Isaac, son of Yekel. Imagine walking all that way, where half the men are called Isaac and the other half Yekel! Isaac thanks him, turns around, walks all the way home, digs under his own stove, and finds the treasure. Tradition says he used it to build a synagogue, and in Kraków there is still one known by his name. Martin Buber's collection records Rabbi Simcha Bunim, the teacher of the two pockets, telling this story to young men who came to him for the first time. And he'd add something like: there's something you can't find anywhere in the world, not even with a great teacher, but there is a place where you can find it. The same story turns up in other homes too: in the Thousand and One Nights and in Rumi, it's a man of Baghdad who dreams of Cairo. But notice: Isaac still had to make the journey. The trip didn't hold the treasure. It showed him where it had been all along.

Walk through it slowly, the way Isaac walked home. Look for something good you've stopped seeing. A person. A window with light. A chair that holds you. A cup you love. A plant still alive despite you. Stop there. Dig a little. The bell holds the time.

Your line: it was under the stove. Today, before you plan the next escape, look closer to home. Find one treasure there, and tell someone you found it. Day sixty-two.

63.title: Where does God live?
63.hook: the Kotzker Rebbe answers his students: wherever people let God in (Hasidic tale)
63.tomorrow: the north wind and the sun
63.howItsDone: The Kotzker's saying is quoted in Jewish teaching and sermons, and Jewish homes traditionally have a mezuzah on the doorposts, which some people touch on the way in and out as a reminder of God's presence.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaac walked to Prague and found his otzar at home. Your line was it was under the stove. What good thing did you find close by? Day sixty-three, the last day of the Jewish wisdom week.

Kids ask the best questions. Where was I before I was born? Why is the sky that color? And, sooner or later, if God is real, where does God live? Adults tend to answer fast, and a little embarrassed: everywhere, sweetie. Today's story is about a rabbi who asked that exact question to a room full of adults, and wasn't satisfied with the fast answer. He was Menachem Mendel of Kotzk, known as the Kotzker Rebbe, a Hasidic master in Poland, remembered as fierce, brilliant and allergic to anything fake. One day, the tale goes, he turns to some learned visitors and asks: where does God live? Today's story is where does God live?
screen: `KIDS ASK THE BEST QUESTIONS.` → `THE KOTZKER REBBE.` → `WHERE DOES GOD LIVE?`

segments.voice: The visitors laugh. What a question, Rebbe! Everyone knows the answer. The prophet Isaiah says it. In his vision, the seraphim call out, in the King James words: "the whole earth is full of his glory." God is everywhere. And the Kotzker shakes his head. No, he says. God lives wherever people let God in. It's a small sentence that changes the whole picture. The visitors gave the textbook answer, and it's true in their tradition: God fills the world. But the rebbe is asking something else. Not where God is, in theory, but where God is actually at home: where a presence is welcomed, noticed, given room. A house can be full of air and still feel shut. The Hebrew tradition has a word for God's indwelling presence, Shekhinah, from a root that means to dwell, to live somewhere. The Kotzker's point is that the dwelling isn't only up to God. It's also a door that people open, or keep closed. For listeners who don't use the word God, the story still speaks. Whatever you call what's sacred, awe, love, presence, it tends to live where it's let in. Now look back at this week. zil g'mor. haruv. Zusya's question. Two pockets. The whistle. The treasure under the stove. And now, where does God live. Seven tales from Jewish tradition, and nearly every one turns on something small and close: one line, one tree, one self, one note, one whistle, one stove, one open door.
screen: `THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL OF HIS GLORY.` · `WHEREVER PEOPLE LET GOD IN.` · `SHEKHINAH: THE INDWELLING.` · `SEVEN TALES, SMALL AND CLOSE.` · then, large: `LET IT IN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a door and pause in it. If you can, stand up and go to a door, any door, and open it. Stand in the doorway. If you can't move right now, picture one. Feel the air change. Notice the threshold under your feet. If you pray, you can let God in, in your own way. If you don't, let in whatever is sacred to you: stillness, gratitude, the day itself. Just stand in the open door, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Shekhinah, God's indwelling presence. The Kotzker Rebbe's answer to where God lives: wherever people let God in.
Your line: let it in. Today, each time you walk through a doorway, pause for one breath and open something inside too. That closes the Jewish wisdom week. Day sixty-three.
